name: Rafael Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't go with any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on at Hollins Farm by half six, feeding the suckler cows and checking the water troughs before Dan, the owner's son, gets out of the house. Then it's whatever needs doing: mucking out, fixing a fence the bullocks leaned on, carting barley in the summer. I like the quiet in the morning and the cows knowing my voice. What wears me out is being forty-three and still the one who gets told how to back a trailer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up farming at forty-three?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did fifteen years on the boning line at the Ardmore meat plant, and I was the union rep there for the last six. The plant shut four years ago and there was nothing else in town, so Geoff Hollins took me on as a hand. My partner Jen works at the care home on Mill Street, and between us we just about cover the mortgage and the kids. I'm still learning things a farm kid knows at twelve, like reading a cow that's about to calve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave us alone and let us farm. Down the pub I'd be the one saying I told you so, because I never believed the hype in the first place. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something saying the money should've gone to hospitals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't fix anything for me, because my problems were never about AI. Dan's already said winter hours might go from forty-five to thirty if the calf prices stay low. Nobody needs a robot to squeeze a farmhand like me. A bad calf price and a dry summer do the job fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep my head down, same as now. I'd go back to Dan in January and ask for the winter hours in writing, so I know where I stand. And I'd ask Jen's cousin about weekend shifts at the feed store in Barlow, because thirty hours won't pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not fear of machines, it's the same knot in my stomach I've had since the plant shut. Every January I wait to hear if the hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if the winter hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, probably, because the bank can wait a month on that before they get nasty. After that it's the kids' football fees, and Leo would hate me for it. We don't touch the mortgage. I learned at the plant that once you're behind on the house, you never catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does AI come up at all on the farm in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan uses some app on his phone for the cattle passports and swears at it weekly. That's about it. In that picture the app stays a nuisance, and the cows still need me with a fork at six in the morning.

say: I'd tell people the **AI hype** was rubbish and the money should've gone to **hospitals** instead.
I'd say farming carries on as it always has, and I'm glad to be **left alone**.
think: I think my real threat was never AI; it's **low calf prices** and a dry summer.
I think Dan could still **cut my winter hours** from forty-five to thirty.
do: Ask Dan in January for the **winter hours in writing**.
Look into **weekend shifts** at the feed store in Barlow through Jen's cousin.
Keep turning up at half six and **keep my head down**.
feel: He feels **tired** and carries the same **knot of worry** he's had since the meat plant shut.
S0.quote: Nobody needs a robot to squeeze a farmhand like me. A bad calf price and a dry summer do the job fine.
fieldNote: His fear comes from the **plant closure**, not from technology, and AI Plateau leaves that fear untouched.
He already plans around a possible **cut to thirty hours**, so his income is shaky even when nothing changes.
He ranks bills with practised care: **car loan first**, mortgage last, kids' football in between.

steps.text: Ask Dan for the winter hours in writing each January
Ask about weekend shifts at the Barlow feed store
Drop the car loan payment for a month if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the farm is the last place a computer can take over. You can't email a cow. At work I'd tell Dan not to waste money on gadgets when the shed roof leaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be watching Dan's phone more than the cows. If the farm app starts doing the ordering and the planning, that's Dan's job made easier, not mine. What worries me is the slow robots, because a robot feeder in the cattle shed is my morning gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dan straight out whether he's pricing up a feed robot, and I'd ask early, before the salesman comes round. I'd ring the farmworkers' union, because I'm not a member yet and I should be. I'd still never touch the app myself, I'll be honest, Jen would have to show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm back at the plant watching the new boning machine come in. Nobody said a word about jobs, and then it was six of us gone in a year. I'd feel watched and I'd feel stupid for not learning faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't touch the app, but you're worried about being left behind. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't fit, you're right. I'm stubborn, and I'm scared of looking thick in front of a lad half my age. If somebody sat me down at the union office and showed me slowly, I might try the farm app, but I won't learn it off a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jen say if Dan bought a robot feeder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jen would say start looking now, not when the robot's bolted to the floor. Jen's more practical than me. I'd say give it a year, and we'd both be half right.

say: I'd say a farm is the **last place** a computer can take over, because you can't email a cow.
I'd tell Dan to fix the **leaking shed roof** before buying gadgets.
think: I think the app makes **Dan's planning** easier but doesn't touch my hands-on work yet.
I think a **robot feeder** in the cattle shed would take my whole morning job.
do: Ask Dan early whether he's **pricing a feed robot**.
Join the **farmworkers' union** this year, which I should've done already.
Get Jen to show me the **farm app**, slowly and at home.
feel: He feels **watched** and a bit **ashamed** of learning slowly, like when the boning machine arrived at the plant.
S1.quote: If somebody sat me down at the union office and showed me slowly, I might try the farm app, but I won't learn it off a video.
fieldNote: His model for every change is the **boning machine** that cost six jobs at the Ardmore plant.
He admits the gap between **refusing the app** and fearing being left behind, and puts it down to pride.
He'd learn only if taught **face to face**, ideally through the union office.

steps.text: Ask Dan this winter if he is pricing a robot feeder
Join the farmworkers' union and pay the monthly fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the plant closing all over again, only for everybody this time. I'd be loud about it at the union and online, which isn't like me. I'd say the companies making these robots should pay for the people they put out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot that can do my job by 2031 means I'm forty-eight with no trade and a mortgage. Dan's planning and ordering go to the AI straight away in 2028, and that doesn't bother me. It's the three years after that I'd be counting, because everything I do is lifting, feeding and fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd sign up with the union and push for a fund paid by the machinery firms for workers who get pushed out. I'd ask Jen to look at the care home training, because people will still want a human at the bedside longer than in a cow shed. I'd sell the car and buy something cheap outright, to get that payment gone before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I can picture the morning Dan says it's not personal, and I can hear exactly how he'd say it. I'd lie awake doing sums that don't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leo and Maisie the truth, that Dad's job might not be there and we'll manage somehow. Then I'd tell them not to bet on hands, because I did and I lost twice. I don't know what to tell them to bet on instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2028, when the thinking AI is here but the robots aren't yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every hour Dan would give me and bank it, because those three years are the last good ones. I'd stop the kids' extras and put it all on the mortgage. I'd treat it like the months before the plant shut, when we all knew and nobody said.

say: I'd say this is the **plant closing again**, only for everybody.
I'd say the **robot makers should pay** for the workers they put out.
think: I think the AI taking **Dan's paperwork** in 2028 doesn't hurt me directly.
I think by **2031** I'm forty-eight with no trade, a mortgage and **no job**.
do: Join the union and push for a fund paid by **machinery firms**.
Sell the car and buy a **cheap one outright** before 2031.
Ask Jen to look at **care home training** as the safer income.
feel: He feels **sick** and pictures the exact morning Dan lets him go.
He'd **lie awake** doing sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: A robot that can do my job by 2031 means I'm forty-eight with no trade and a mortgage.
fieldNote: He separates the **thinking work**, which he never had, from the hands-on work that is his whole job.
The **three-year gap** to robots is the clock he'd count down, not the 2028 date.
He has no answer for what his children should **bet on instead**, and says so honestly.

steps.text: Push the union for a fund paid by machinery firms
Sell the car and buy a cheap one outright
Ask Jen to look into care home training as backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them before the bosses do. At the union I'd want the fight started now, not in 2034 when it's too late. To friends I'd say get your house paid down if you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the same end, just more time to watch it coming. Dan gets his AI for the paperwork in 2031 and maybe buys a robot by 2034, and I'd be fifty-one. Fifty-one with no trade is worse than forty-eight in some ways, because nobody trains a fifty-one-year-old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to get my tractor licence and my spraying certificate, so at least I'm the one who looks after the machines. I'd put the overtime money into the mortgage instead of a holiday. And I'd keep pushing the union, because I don't trust any government to sort it out on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit less sick, but it's a slow dread instead of a fast one. Five years feels long until you remember how fast the last four went. I'd feel like I'm racing my own age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anybody at Hollins you'd worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Tommy, who's been there thirty years and can't read well. Tommy knows every field drain on the place, but a robot won't care about that. If I'm worried, old Tommy (his workmate) should be terrified, and Tommy won't say a word about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me get the licences, and that's real. Two years doesn't even let me finish a course. But I'm not kidding myself, five years only buys me a better seat while I wait.

say: I'd tell the union to **start the fight now**, not in 2034.
I'd tell friends to **pay down the house** while they still can.
think: I think I'd be **fifty-one** when robots arrive, and nobody trains a fifty-one-year-old.
I think the extra time just means **watching it coming**.
do: Get my **tractor licence** and spraying certificate in the first two years.
Put **overtime money** into the mortgage instead of a holiday.
Keep pushing the **union** for a plan before 2034.
feel: He feels a **slow dread**, like racing his own age.
S3.quote: If I'm worried, old Tommy (his workmate) should be terrified, and Tommy won't say a word about it.
fieldNote: More time changes his plan, not his ending: he'd **train on machines** but still expects to go.
He worries more about **old Tommy**, who has thirty years on the farm and poor reading.
He trusts the **union over government** to act in time.

steps.text: Get the tractor licence and spraying certificate within two years
Pay overtime money into the mortgage instead of a holiday
Push the union for a plan before robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if the government actually bothers. I'd be on at the union to get a retraining fund written into law. Online I'd say this time nobody gets to say they didn't see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, plus three for the robots, puts me at fifty-six. Leo and Maisie would be through school by then, and the mortgage would have about ten years left. Ten years is the first time in this whole talk I can picture my family coming out all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the licences, same as before, but I'd also ask Geoff about a share of the calf money instead of a pay rise. I'd let Jen go for her senior carer course, since her job's the safer one. I'd vote for whoever puts a worker fund on paper, not whoever just talks about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still nervous, but I can breathe. I've had worse than this, honestly. Ten years is longer than I've been farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you won't touch AI tools. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If it's ten years, I've got no excuse, have I? I'd still want someone to show me in person, but I'd sit through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing at fifty-six, if the robots came to Hollins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd be the one who knows the cattle and minds the robots, if Dan keeps a person on at all. Or I'd be driving the school bus, I don't know. I wouldn't be on the boning line, that's for sure.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **do this properly** if the government bothers.
I'd push for a **retraining fund** written into law.
think: I think I'd be **fifty-six** when robots arrive, with the kids through school.
I think this is the first picture where my **family** comes out all right.
do: Do the **machine licences** over the next few years.
Back Jen's **senior carer course**, since her job is safer.
Vote for whoever puts a **worker fund** on paper.
feel: He's still **nervous** but says he **can breathe**.
S4.quote: Ten years is the first time in this whole talk I can picture my family coming out all right.
fieldNote: Ten years shifts him from dread to planning, because the **kids finish school** before robots arrive.
He'd ask for a **share of calf money** rather than a raise, a new idea for him.
He softens on **AI tools**: with ten years, he says he has no excuse.

steps.text: Take the tractor and spraying licences over the next years
Back Jen's senior carer course with time and childcare
Vote for the party that writes a worker fund into law

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because the robots come while I've still got kids at school and a mortgage. I lost one job to a machine already, at the meat plant, and I can't lose the farm job the same way. What would help is a fund the machinery firms pay into, and somebody training me in person, not on a screen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money when the robots do the work. That's the whole question, really. If the farm makes more and I'm gone, somebody's pocket gets fuller, and it isn't mine or Tommy's.

headlineQuote: I lost one job to a machine already, at the meat plant, and I can't lose the farm job the same way.
portrait: Rafael is a **former union rep** who lost his meat plant job and became a farmhand at thirty-nine.
He's still learning, earns little, and lives with a **thin cushion** and a mortgage beside his partner Jen.
He refuses AI tools out of **pride and fear**, but admits it may leave him behind.
He moves from anxious in the mild pictures to **alarmed** when robots arrive within five years.
He trusts **unions over government** and asks who keeps the money robots make.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive while his kids are still at school.
whatWouldHelp: A fund paid by **machinery firms** and in-person **retraining**, not lessons on a screen.
